candidates.question: Within U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211), how large are the hourly wage gaps between renewable generation industries (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass) and non-renewable generation industries (fossil fuel and nuclear), do these gaps persist within detailed occupations, how do they differ across individual energy sources and occupational groups, and how did they change between 2021 and 2025?
candidates.mechanism: Legacy fossil and nuclear generation is a mature, capital-intensive, heavily regulated and comparatively unionized segment with large incumbent firms and rent-sharing, whereas the newer solar and wind segments are younger, more contractor- and developer-based, less unionized and have flatter internal labor markets; establishment wage-setting rather than occupational skill should therefore produce within-occupation wage gaps that may narrow as renewable segments mature and as IRA prevailing-wage provisions take effect.
confounders: skill and education requirements embedded in occupations
geographic location of plants (not observable nationally)
firm size and union coverage (not observable)

scope.population: occupation-by-industry employment cells in U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211, eight six-digit generation industries)
scope.unit: detailed SOC occupation x six-digit generation industry x year cell

candidates.recommended_dataset: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) national industry-specific estimates, May 2021-May 2025, NAICS 221111-221118
candidates.novelty_risk: low-medium: prior U.S. work compares green vs. non-green jobs economy-wide or via postings and linked admin data (Curtis and Marinescu; Colmer et al.), not within-occupation gaps across generation sources inside one industry over 2021-2025

candidates.question: How much of the raw wage gap between renewable and non-renewable power generation industries is explained by differences in occupational composition versus within-occupation pay differences, and has that split changed from 2021 to 2025?
candidates.mechanism: Renewable plants employ more sales, construction and technician occupations and fewer high-paid plant operators and engineers; composition versus wage-setting.

scope.population: occupation-by-industry employment cells in U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211, eight six-digit generation industries)
scope.unit: detailed SOC occupation x six-digit generation industry x year cell

candidates.novelty_risk: medium: decomposition alone is a narrower contribution

candidates.question: Is within-occupation wage dispersion (90/10 percentile ratio) larger in renewable than in fossil and nuclear generation, and did dispersion converge over 2021-2025?
candidates.y: log 90/10 hourly wage ratio within occupation-industry cells
candidates.mechanism: Less standardized pay structures and lower union coverage in new segments produce wider dispersion.

scope.population: occupation-by-industry employment cells in U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211, eight six-digit generation industries)
scope.unit: detailed SOC occupation x six-digit generation industry x year cell

candidates.question: Did faster employment growth in solar and wind generation between 2021 and 2025 raise relative wages in those industries (a labor-demand effect)?
candidates.mechanism: Demand-driven wage pressure in expanding segments.

scope.population: occupation-by-industry employment cells in U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211, eight six-digit generation industries)
scope.unit: detailed SOC occupation x six-digit generation industry x year cell

candidates.fatal_flaw_reason: Eight industries and overlapping three-year OEWS sample panels cannot identify a causal demand effect; causal claim exceeds design.
